title: Gerund or Infinitive After Verb? The Complete List for Bank PO Exams
excerpt: Eight out of ten Bank PO aspirants lose easy marks not because they don't know grammar — but because they guess between 'enjoy swimming' and 'enjoy to swim' by ear. Here is the complete, memorizable list that ends the guessing forever.
author: Balu Kandekar
content:
Stop guessing. That's the first thing I tell every batch. 'I enjoy swimming' is correct. 'I enjoy to swim' is not. And no, it's not because 'swimming' sounds nicer — it's because 'enjoy' belongs to a fixed list of verbs that only accept a gerund, never an infinitive. If you've ever second-guessed yourself between 'want to go' and 'want going' in the middle of a Bank PO paper, this post is going to fix that confusion permanently.

Quick Answer: Some verbs in English (like enjoy, avoid, and finish) are always followed by a gerund (V-ing), while others (like want, decide, and hope) are always followed by an infinitive (to + verb). There is no shortcut around memorizing which verb belongs to which group — but a list of the 40 highest-frequency exam verbs, sorted by pattern, makes the job manageable in a single sitting.

Why This Trips Up Even Strong Students

Here's the part nobody tells you in a regular classroom: gerund-versus-infinitive isn't really a grammar rule in the way subject-verb agreement is. There's no logical test you can apply mid-exam. It's a matter of which verbs, by convention, "go with" which structure — and that convention has to be memorized, not derived.

This is exactly why so many aspirants who are otherwise strong in tenses and articles still stumble here. They're looking for a rule where there is only a pattern. And in a 60-second-per-question exam like IBPS PO Prelims, there's no time to sit and reason it out — you either know the verb's pattern instantly, or you lose the mark.

  • You've memorized 10-15 verbs, but the exam picks the one you missed.
  • You confuse 'stop to do' with 'stop doing' — and they mean completely different things.
  • You freeze on verbs like 'like', 'love', 'prefer' that can technically take both, but shift meaning slightly.
  • You've never seen the full list organized by pattern, only scattered examples in different books.

But here's what most people get wrong: they try to memorize gerund/infinitive rules through isolated sentences instead of grouped lists. Grouping is what makes this stick.

The 3 Mistakes That Cost the Most Marks

Mistake 1: Treating 'stop', 'remember', and 'try' like fixed-pattern verbs.
These three are the most dangerous verbs in this entire topic because they change meaning depending on which form follows them. 'I stopped to smoke' means I paused another activity in order to smoke. 'I stopped smoking' means I quit the habit entirely. Students memorize one version and apply it everywhere — and lose marks on both.

Mistake 2: Assuming 'suggest' takes an infinitive because it "feels" like a request.
'Suggest' is a gerund-only verb — 'He suggested going early', never 'he suggested to go early'. Aspirants confuse it with 'want' or 'advise', which do take infinitives, because all three verbs semantically involve telling someone to do something.

Mistake 3: Forgetting that a preposition before a verb always forces a gerund.
'Look forward to', 'good at', 'interested in' — whenever a preposition sits directly before a verb, that verb must be in the -ing form, no exceptions. 'I am interested to learn' is a very common wrong answer choice in Bank PO papers specifically because it sounds acceptable in spoken English.

Common Mistakes Students Make

❌
Mistake 1: Treating 'stop' as a fixed-pattern verb

'Stop + infinitive' and 'stop + gerund' mean completely different things.

Wrong meaning mix-up: I stopped to smoke = quit smoking (INCORRECT)

Correct: I stopped smoking = quit the habit

❌
Mistake 2: Giving 'suggest' an infinitive

'Suggest' is gerund-only, confused with request verbs like 'advise'.

Wrong: He suggested to go early.

Correct: He suggested going early.

❌
Mistake 3: Forgetting the preposition-forces-gerund rule

A preposition right before a verb always forces the -ing form.

Wrong: I am interested to learn.

Correct: I am interested in learning.

The Solution: 5 Grouped Lists That Actually Stick

Step 1: Memorize the Gerund-Only Group First.
These 12 verbs are always followed by V-ing and never by 'to + verb': enjoy, avoid, finish, suggest, admit, deny, mind, risk, postpone, delay, practice, resist. Read them out loud as a chant three times a day for a week — this single group covers roughly 30% of gerund/infinitive questions in SSC and Bank exams.

❌ She admitted to steal the documents.
✅ She admitted stealing the documents.

Step 2: Memorize the Infinitive-Only Group Second.
These 12 verbs are always followed by 'to + verb': want, decide, hope, plan, promise, refuse, agree, manage, afford, fail, offer, seem.

❌ He refused signing the form.
✅ He refused to sign the form.

Step 3: Isolate the Meaning-Changing Verbs.
Only four verbs genuinely change meaning depending on the form used: stop, remember, forget, try. Learn these as pairs, not as a single rule — because a single rule will actively mislead you here.

  • Remember to lock the door (don't forget to do it — future obligation) vs Remember locking the door (recall having done it — past memory)
  • Try to open the jar (attempt something difficult) vs Try opening the jar under hot water (experiment with a method)

Step 4: Learn the Preposition-Forces-Gerund Rule as a Single Universal Law.
Whenever 'to' functions as a preposition rather than part of an infinitive, it must be followed by a gerund. This covers 'look forward to', 'object to', 'used to' (in the habitual sense), 'with a view to', 'in addition to', and every adjective + preposition combination like 'good at', 'keen on', 'interested in'.

❌ I look forward to meet you.
✅ I look forward to meeting you.

Step 5: Drill With Real Sentence Completion Format Under Time Pressure.
Grammar knowledge that only exists on paper doesn't transfer to a 60-second exam question. Once you know the four groups, time yourself doing 20 fill-in-the-blank questions in under 8 minutes. Speed under pressure is what separates knowing the rule from being able to use it.

Step-by-Step Strategy

1
Memorize the Gerund-Only Group

enjoy, avoid, finish, suggest, admit, deny, mind, risk, postpone, delay, practice, resist.

Example: She admitted stealing the documents.

2
Memorize the Infinitive-Only Group

want, decide, hope, plan, promise, refuse, agree, manage, afford, fail, offer, seem.

Example: He refused to sign the form.

3
Isolate Meaning-Changing Verbs

stop, remember, forget, try — learn as contrasting pairs, not as one rule.

Example: Remember to lock the door vs Remember locking the door.

4
Apply the Preposition-Forces-Gerund Law

'to' as a preposition, plus every adjective + preposition combo, needs V-ing.

Example: I look forward to meeting you.

5
Drill Under Timed Conditions

Speed transfers knowledge into exam-ready recall — aim for 20 questions in 8 minutes.

A Quick Story: How One Student Turned This Around

One of my long-time online students, preparing for IBPS PO, kept losing 2-3 marks every mock test on exactly this topic — not because she didn't study grammar, but because she was learning gerund/infinitive rules the same way she learned tenses: as logic, not as memorized groups. Once she rewrote the four lists on a single index card and drilled them for ten minutes daily for two weeks, her error-spotting accuracy on this topic went from roughly 50% to nearly perfect in her next three mocks. Nothing else changed in her preparation — just the shift from 'understanding' to 'memorizing in groups'. You can do the same — here's how to start.

Expert Tips From 22 Years in the Classroom

  • Write the two core lists on your exam-day revision sheet — not the whole grammar book, just these 24 verbs. This is the highest-return five minutes you can spend the night before an exam.
  • Say sentences out loud, not just read them. Verb-pattern memory is closer to muscle memory than logical memory — students who read silently forget faster than students who whisper example sentences to themselves.
  • Never trust how a sentence 'sounds' in spoken English. Spoken Indian English regularly uses 'interested to know' and 'suggested to go' — both wrong in written exam grammar. Your ear is not a reliable examiner here.
  • Test yourself with fill-in-the-blank, not multiple choice, while practicing. Multiple choice lets you recognize the answer; fill-in-the-blank forces you to recall it — and recall is what the actual exam demands.

The Bottom Line

Gerund-versus-infinitive is not a rule you can reason your way through in an exam hall — it's a pattern you either know cold or don't know at all. The good news is that just 24-30 verbs, grouped correctly, cover the overwhelming majority of what SSC CGL, IBPS PO, and similar exams actually test. Learn the groups, drill them daily for two weeks, and this entire topic stops being a source of lost marks.

Q1 (SSC CGL Exam Pattern): The committee postponed _______ (announce) the results until next week.

Answer: announcing

Explanation: 'Postpone' belongs to the Gerund-Only Group (Step 1), so it must always be followed by V-ing.

Q2 (Bank PO Exam Pattern): She is not interested _______ (join) the new project team.

Answer: in joining

Explanation: 'Interested' pairs with the preposition 'in', and Step 4's Preposition-Forces-Gerund Law means the verb after it must take the -ing form.

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)

Q1. Is there a shortcut trick to know if a verb takes a gerund or infinitive?
No single trick covers every verb — it must be memorized as grouped lists. However, one reliable pattern is that any verb following a preposition (including 'to' used as a preposition) always takes a gerund.
Q2. Why do 'stop', 'remember', 'forget', and 'try' behave differently from other verbs?
These four verbs genuinely change meaning depending on whether a gerund or infinitive follows, which is why they must be learned as contrasting pairs rather than fixed-pattern verbs.
Q3. Can 'like', 'love', and 'prefer' take both gerund and infinitive?
Yes, both forms are grammatically acceptable with these verbs, though the infinitive form often implies a specific occasion while the gerund implies a general preference.
Q4. How many gerund/infinitive verbs do I actually need to memorize for SSC CGL and Bank PO?
Around 24 to 30 high-frequency verbs, split across the Gerund-Only Group, the Infinitive-Only Group, and the small set of meaning-changing verbs, cover the large majority of questions asked in these exams.
Q5. Is 'used to' always followed by a gerund?
Only when 'used to' functions as an adjective phrase meaning 'accustomed to' (e.g., 'used to waking up early'). When 'used to' expresses a past habit that no longer continues, it is followed by the base verb, not a gerund (e.g., 'I used to wake up early').
